Non-Euclidean Geometry. Geometric systems that do not satisfy Euclid's parallel postulate.

The parallel postulate states that through a point not on a line, exactly one parallel line exists. In hyperbolic geometry, infinitely many parallels exist. In elliptic geometry, none do. These alternative geometries were developed in the nineteenth century by Gauss privately and by Lobachevsky and Bolyai publicly. They were later proven consistent by Poincaré's models. The discovery shattered the notion that Euclidean geometry was the only true geometry and paved the way for Einstein's curved spacetime in relativity.

For two thousand years, mathematicians tried unsuccessfully to derive the parallel postulate from Euclid's other four postulates. In hyperbolic geometry, multiple distinct parallel lines exist through a point not on a given line. The sum of angles in a triangle is less than one hundred eighty degrees. Parallel lines diverge indefinitely. In elliptic geometry, no parallel lines exist. All lines eventually intersect. The sum of angles in a triangle is greater than one hundred eighty degrees. The geometry is bounded with finite total area, like a sphere's surface.

The surface of a sphere exhibits elliptic properties. Geodesics, or shortest paths, are great circles. Parallel lines always intersect at the poles. Poincaré's half-plane model represents hyperbolic geometry as the upper half-plane with a specific metric, showing hyperbolic geometry is internally consistent. Non-Euclidean spaces have intrinsic curvature. Euclidean space has zero curvature. Hyperbolic space has negative curvature. Elliptic space has positive curvature.

Carl Friedrich Gauss privately developed non-Euclidean geometry but never published, fearing controversy. His unpublished notes reveal he had explored the subject decades before public breakthroughs. The existence of consistent non-Euclidean geometries overturned centuries of philosophical certainty. They proved that mathematical systems could differ profoundly yet remain internally consistent. This revelation influenced the foundations of mathematics, physics, and philosophy.
